claim_verdicts.evidence: git show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Controllers/ProductsController.cs, lines 13-20: "[HttpGet] public async Task<ActionResult<List<ProductDto>>> List() { var products = await db.Products.Select(p => new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceVnd)).ToListAsync(); return Ok(products); }". One return statement, no if/ternary/count check anywhere in the method body, so row count cannot influence the status code.

Source lines 22-28: "var product = await db.Products.FindAsync(id); if (product is null) return NotFound(); return Ok(new ProductDto(product.Id, product.Name, product.PriceVnd));" — the null branch returns before the ProductDto constructor runs. Executed against the running lab: GET /api/v1/products/1 -> "HTTP/1.1 200 OK ... {"id":1,"name":"Bàn phím cơ","priceVnd":1250000}"; GET /api/v1/products/999999 -> "HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found".

Body carries no product, but it is not empty — see issue on section 7.

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §9.2.1: "Request methods are considered 'safe' if their defined semantics are essentially read-only; i.e., the client does not request, and does not expect, any state change on the origin server"; and "This definition of safe methods does not prevent an implementation from including behavior... that causes side effects". §9.2.2: "PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent" — safe does imply idempotent, but "must not change server state" is stronger than the standard allows.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: By HTTP convention GET is a safe method: the client does not request and does not expect any change to the resource, and safe methods are also idempotent, so safe is the stronger of the two promises.

issues.text: Contradicted by the governing standard. RFC 9110 §9.2.1 says the safe-method definition "does not prevent an implementation from including behavior that... causes side effects", giving access logging and "charging an advertising account" as safe examples; §9.2.2 adds "a server is free to log each request separately". A server-side view counter the client never asked for is not, by itself, a breach of GET's semantics; writing to the resource the client asked to read is.
issues.quote: A GET method that logged a view count, marked something as read, or changed a row would still be answering the right status codes and still be violating this rule
issues.fix: Restate the rule around what the client requested: "A GET must not change the resources it serves — the client asked to read, not to write." Drop "logged a view count" from the list of violations (logging is explicitly safe) and keep the two unambiguous cases: "marked something as read, or changed a row".

issues.text: Unlisted claim: the lesson's central 200/404 rule for collection URLs is stated as unconditional fact but appears nowhere in .meta.json claims (claims 1-3 are about the code, claim 5 about safety). No HTTP standard mandates it: RFC 9110 defines neither "collection URL" nor a status code for an empty result set; it is a REST convention. "always" is also false outside the found/not-found question (401, 403, 500 are all possible answers to a collection GET).
issues.quote: collection GET always `200` — a collection URL names the whole set, and the set still exists even with zero members in it right now
issues.fix: Add this to .meta.json claims (kind behavior). In the bullet and in summary line 2, scope the rule: "a collection GET answers `200` whatever the row count — an empty set is still a successful answer, never a `404`". Drop the bare "always".

issues.text: Unlisted claim: the definition of `404` is given as fact but is not in the claims ledger, and it is narrower than the standard. RFC 9110 §15.5.5: "The 404 (Not Found) status code indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists." "Does not exist" excludes the hidden-resource case and asserts more about the world than a 404 actually does.
issues.quote: `404` means the one specific thing the URL named does not exist
issues.fix: Add the claim to .meta.json (kind behavior, source RFC 9110 §15.5.5) and soften to: "`404` means the server has nothing to return for the one specific thing the URL named." Apply the same wording to summary line 1 and to quiz q1 option a.

issues.text: The expected result understates what the learner sees. The 404 response is not bodiless: observed at stage-1, Content-Type is application/problem+json and the body is {"type":"https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc9110#section-15.5.5","title":"Not Found","status":404,"traceId":"..."}. A reader told "no product in the body" who then sees a JSON object will think the lab disagrees with the lesson.
issues.quote: the second returns `404`, with no product in the body
issues.fix: Write: "the second returns `404`; its body is a short JSON error description with no product data in it". Keep the rest of the sentence unchanged.

issues.text: Ambiguous ordering. Option c ("The response body has no product in it") is a property of the response, option d ("The client reads a `404` status line") a client-side event; on the wire the status line arrives before the body, so a learner ordering by what the client sees will answer a, b, d, c. Only the server-side reading of c makes the key a, b, c, d unique.
issues.quote: The response body has no product in it
issues.fix: Reword option c to a server-side event: "`NotFound()` produces a response whose body carries no product". The key a, b, c, d then stays correct and unambiguous.

issues.text: Distractor b is defensible under the standard the lesson leans on. RFC 9110 §9.2.1 treats side effects the client did not request (logging, charging an ad account) as compatible with a safe method, so "Nothing is wrong, as long as the response still correctly returns 200 or 404" is arguably right for a view counter. The key a is only correct under the lesson's stronger-than-RFC phrasing flagged in the section 4 issue.
issues.quote: Nothing is wrong, as long as the response still correctly returns `200` or `404`
issues.fix: After fixing section 4, reword b to be unambiguously wrong: "Nothing is wrong: a GET may write to the data it serves whenever the status code is still right." Keep the key as a.
